Since $d \mid \ell - 1$ (Fermat), we get $2^{a+1} \mid \ell - 1$. Applying this to both $p$ and $q$:
$$p \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{a+1}}, \quad q \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{a+1}} \implies 2^{a+1} \mid (q - p).$$

But $(q-p) \mid m = 2^a \cdot t$ forces $2^{a+1} \mid 2^a \cdot t$, i.e., $2 \mid t$. This contradicts $t$ being odd. $\square$

## Step 2: $n = 1$ is excluded

$1^m + 1 = 2$ for all $m$, which has only one prime divisor. So $1 \notin S$.

So $n \in S$. $\square$
